hyperbole

hy-PUR-buh-lee -- from Greek hyperbole, 'excess,' from hyper- (over) + ballein (to throw): hyperbole 'throws' language over the top. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Hyperbole is a deliberately exaggerated statement, not meant to be taken literally.

Saying the school cafeteria's pizza was 'the greatest meal in the history of the world' was pure hyperbole, but nobody could stop laughing.

Example

After waiting in line for eleven minutes, the customer reached for hyperbole, dramatically announcing that he had 'aged a full decade' standing there.

Hyperbole means stretching the truth on purpose for effect, not because anyone actually believes it -- nobody thinks eleven minutes truly ages a person a decade, but saying so makes the frustration funny and vivid.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

overstatement: An overstatement is any claim that goes beyond the facts, and the word itself stays neutral, even formal -- an auditor can note an overstatement of earnings without a hint of humor. Hyperbole is overstatement worn openly as a device: theatrical, deliberately unbelievable, built to amuse or emphasize.

embellishment: An embellishment decorates a story with invented or polished details -- the borrowed suit becomes designer, polite applause becomes a roar -- and it is meant to be believed. Hyperbole does not decorate; it blows a single claim up to an impossible size that no listener could take literally.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

understatement: a statement that describes something as smaller than it really is

fact: a statement that is objectively true

Where it sits · how deliberately the truth is stretched — exaggeration → hyperbole → tall tale

exaggeration vs. hyperbole: Exaggeration is the broadest, most everyday word for stretching the truth, while hyperbole specifically names it as a deliberate rhetorical device.

tall tale vs. hyperbole: A tall tale goes further than hyperbole -- not one deliberately stretched claim but a whole story spun past believing, every detail inflated on purpose for the fun of it.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — hyper-

prefix — hyper-: over, beyond, excessive (Greek)

root — -bole-

root — -bole-: a throw, a casting (Greek ballein ('to throw'))

Put it together

Put it together: Hyperbole comes from Greek hyperbole, 'excess,' from hyper- ('over, beyond') plus ballein ('to throw') -- it literally means to 'throw beyond' the truth, the same prefix behind hyperactive.

Use the root in a new word: symbol

Use the root in a new word: symbol: A dove is a symbol of peace, two ideas 'thrown together' in the Greek sense so that one instantly calls up the other.
